Recent benchmark evaluations increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as automatic judges. This paradigm assumes LLMs evaluate based on the rubric's semantic meaning rather than its numeric scale. We question this assumption by introducing semantic faithfulness: the principle that semantically equivalent rubrics must yield consistent scores. To quantify this, we propose a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without altering evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we introduce floor normalization to calibrate reversal disagreement against intrinsic model variability, enabling fair cross-model comparisons. Experiments across five meta-evaluation benchmarks with seven diverse LLM judges spanning open-weight and proprietary models reveal widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, showing that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirectional anchor averaging reduces dependence on any single anchor direction without compromising alignment with human judgments. Our findings emphasize that trustworthy LLM judges must reliably follow rubric semantics, not just correlate with human ratings.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate other models’ outputs in medicine, an approach known as LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ), yet no LaaJ-specific reporting checklist exists. This scoping review included 91 medical LaaJ studies: 69 from 5,571 database records and 22 from a previous review. Judges were mainly used for response evaluation (74.7%), and 76.9% of the studies used at least one proprietary LLM. Agreement with human evaluators was reported in 65.9% of the studies, with widely varying metrics. Based on these findings, this study developed RULE-LLM, a reporting framework of 21 items and eight sub-items across four domains: role and task specification, underlying data and criteria, LLM-Judge design and output, and evaluation of judge performance. Seven experts rated the initial draft (S-CVI/Ave, 0.94), and five independent raters showed substantial agreement when applying the final framework (Fleiss' κ, 0.67; Gwet's AC1, 0.73). RULE-LLM aims to improve the transparency and reproducibility of LaaJ studies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of app-based food delivery has intensified concerns about riders’ road safety and occupational health. This scoping review maps and synthesises existing research on the safety of food delivery riders, including its methodological characteristics, multilevel determinants, safety and health outcomes, and prevention approaches. Following the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and TRID were searched for English-language sources published from 2013 to 2026. After duplicate removal and two stage screening, 198 sources were included and synthesised through descriptive mapping and thematic analysis. The evidence comprised surveys, interviews, observations, naturalistic riding studies, platform data, and retrospective hospital and crash records. The evidence base was dominated by cross-sectional and self-reported research. Research activity in this field surged from 2022. Findings indicate that rider safety and health are shaped by interacting determinants at four levels: individual characteristics; work and platform conditions; road, vehicle, and environmental conditions; and institutional and social protection. Reported outcomes extended beyond risky riding, crashes, and traffic injuries to include musculoskeletal symptoms, fatigue, sleep disturbance, environmental exposure, and psychological distress. Only a small proportion of studies evaluated implemented interventions, leaving the effectiveness of platform, infrastructure, and policy level measures uncertain. Current evidence remains geographically concentrated, methodologically heterogeneous, and limited in its capacity to establish causal relationships. Improving rider safety therefore requires a shared, systems-based approach involving riders, platforms, restaurants, customers, transport authorities, and labour regulators, alongside longitudinal, exposure-adjusted, and intervention focused research.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as automated evaluators to reduce the cost and time required for human annotation. However, the role of scoring-scheme design in the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation remains underexplored. To address this problem, we introduce numerical scoring topology, which characterizes the structural design of a scoring scheme in terms of its scale width, granularity, offset, symmetry, and boundary placement. Building on this definition, we conduct the first systematic study of how numerical scoring topology influences zero-shot LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation across diverse benchmarks and judge models. Our results show that numerical scoring topology systematically affects judge scores, calibration, and robustness, particularly in judgment-intensive evaluations. Shifted and narrow ranges tend to induce some of the largest score deviations across many settings. We further find that stronger and larger judge models generally achieve higher discriminative validity and greater robustness to scoring-topology changes. These findings suggest that numerical scoring topology should be treated as an integral component of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation and highlight the need for more principled and standardized scoring protocols.

Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted. We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. Specifically, the ANALYST performs a software security assessment while SCARVA records every tool call, file access, and web request. Then, one or more independent JUDGE agents inspect the ANALYST's result and produce an evidence-backed report. We evaluate SCARVA on 54 manually curated cases, balanced across exploitable, non-exploitable, and vulnerability-free projects, using both open-weight and frontier models. The best ANALYST model, Qwen 3.8, reaches 82% balanced accuracy and surpasses the evaluated proprietary models. Human annotation validates the JUDGE findings: Claude Opus 5.5 performs best, agreeing with annotators in 94% of claim checks. Finally, we discuss the most common failure modes of agents on supply-chain vulnerability assessment.

Science communication leverages online multimedia to raise public awareness of research and discovery, yet its efficacy is built upon digital competencies, communication and storytelling. These skills sit outside the scope of traditional scientific training, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools can accelerate professional learning in service of public outreach. Three different AI prompting strategies were used to convert a research article written by the author to a format appropriate for a public lecture. Different titles, graphics, and a talk outline informed by the Three Act Storytelling framework were extracted from the paper using one-shot, chain of thought and role-prompting strategies. These resources can be re-purposed for video abstracts, lay summaries and social media posts to facilitate science communication to a broad generalist audience. The effectiveness of AI as a collaborative tool for ideation is considered alongside its impact on scientific credibility and graduate employability.

Education 5.0 places human agency, ethical technology use, critical thinking, creativity, and meaningful learning at the centre of digital transformation. In higher education, this shift requires institutions to develop not only technological infrastructure but also the research and information literacies needed to evaluate AI-mediated knowledge. Scite.ai is an AI-enabled scholarly citation-intelligence platform that extends conventional citation indexing by displaying citation context and classifying citation statements as supporting, contrasting, or mentioning. This chapter critically examines how Scite can contribute to AI readiness, research literacy, evidence evaluation, and responsible academic practice within an Education 5.0 ecosystem. An integrative review approach is used to synthesize Scite-specific research with literature on Education 5.0, AI literacy, information literacy, technology acceptance, human-centred AI, academic integrity, and institutional governance. The chapter argues that Scite should not be positioned as an automated authority or replacement for scholarly reading. Rather, it can function as an evidence-navigation and critical-reading layer within a broader institutional learning ecosystem. A new institutional conceptual framework is proposed in which Education 5.0 provides the normative context; institutional and stakeholder readiness provide enabling conditions; technology acceptance influences use; Scite-supported practices provide research affordances; and AI literacy, information literacy, critical evaluation, and evidence synthesis mediate potential outcomes. The framework is operationalized through a six-stage institutional roadmap: diagnose, prepare, pilot, integrate, evaluate, and scale. The chapter also identifies risks related to classification error, incomplete coverage, contextual ambiguity, automation bias, privacy, affordability, and academic integrity. The central conclusion is that the educational value of Scite depends less on automation itself than on the quality of human-AI interaction, pedagogical design, verification practices, and institutional governance surrounding its use.

Deploying fruit instance segmentation in real agricultural settings requires generalizing across unseen species, orchards, and imaging conditions under strict onboard compute and annotation budgets. We introduce SegAnyFruit (SAF), a data construction and progressive training framework that distills foundation-model priors into lightweight, prompt-free segmenters. SAF combines generic mask pre-training, broad mid-training on automatically annotated web imagery from our curated WebFruits dataset, and human-verified agricultural refinement post-training on PaperFruits, together spanning 733K images and 9.66M whole-fruit masks across 165 fruit types. Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL reaches 69.06 average mask AP50:95 (+4.76 over SAM 3) while remaining deployable on edge devices. SAF initialization also boosts few-shot to full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we systematically analyze training stages, data scale, model capacity, and generative augmentation, and validate our pipeline's transferability to underwater, cell, and human segmentation. We will release our datasets, code, and SAF models.

Introduction: Mobile pre-hospital care plays a fundamental role in emergency and urgent healthcare assistance, being responsible for rapid and decisive interventions in life-threatening situations. In this context, health professionals working in Mobile Intensive Care Units are constantly exposed to different occupational risks, including biological, physical, ergonomic and psychosocial hazards resulting from the dynamic and unpredictable conditions of the work environment. Objective: To analyze the factors related to the safety of health professionals working in mobile pre-hospital care, with emphasis on occupational risks present in Mobile Intensive Care Units. Methodology: This is an integrative literature review, with a descriptive character and qualitative approach, carried out in the databases Virtual Health Library, LILACS, BDENF, SciELO and PubMed/MEDLINE. Full scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025, in Portuguese, English and Spanish, related to the proposed theme, were included. Results and Discussions: The analyzed studies showed that professionals working in mobile pre-hospital care are frequently exposed to accidents involving biological material, urban violence, traffic accidents, physical exhaustion, emotional overload and high levels of occupational stress. Furthermore, inadequate working conditions, insufficient material resources and limitations related to continuous training contribute to increasing the occupational vulnerability of these teams. On the other hand, the studies highlighted the importance of biosafety measures, proper use of Personal Protective Equipment, continuing education and strengthening institutional policies aimed at workers' health. Final considerations: It is concluded that occupational risks present in mobile pre-hospital care directly impact the health and quality of life of professionals, highlighting the need to strengthen protection strategies and occupational health promotion in urgent and emergency healthcare services.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence transforms self-correction from a localized answer-revision problem into a system-level reliability and recovery challenge. In autonomous, stateful, and long-horizon systems, early errors can propagate through reasoning, planning, retrieval, tool use, external actions, multi-agent interaction, and persistent memory. However, existing research often treats self-correction as either response-level refinement or a capability within broader agent architectures. This study develops an agent-level perspective that connects these fragmented views. It distinguishes reasoning, reflection, verification, correction, and adaptation, emphasizing that reasoning or critique alone does not constitute self-correction unless evaluative information produces a subsequent behavioral change. The study introduces a unified corrective lifecycle covering anomaly detection, error diagnosis and localization, corrective evidence acquisition, repair, validation, commitment or rollback, memory updating, and continuation, termination, or escalation. Existing approaches are organized across five dimensions: correction target, feedback source, temporal scope, persistence, and control architecture. A comparative synthesis shows that self-correction is not uniformly beneficial: repeated reflection can improve performance, stagnate, or degrade initially correct behavior. More reliable gains generally arise when feedback is task-relevant, informative, and at least partially independent of the process that produced the error. The study also identifies key failure modes, including missed errors, unsuccessful repair, over-correction, error amplification, memory contamination, and objective misalignment. These findings motivate research on calibrated intervention, memory integrity, verification, rollback, cost-aware correction, human escalation, and resilience under distribution shift.

Basketball play-by-play data provide semi-structured descriptions of game events, but connecting analytical queries to the corresponding moments in broadcast video remains challenging. Towards this direction, this paper presents a semantic framework that integrates basketball play-by-play information into a Knowledge Graph (KG) through the BBall ontology, and links recorded events to temporally grounded video segments using scoreboard-based optical character recognition (OCR). The framework supports multimodal exploitation using structured queries over game events, through the research prototype CourtLens. The latter enables users to retrieve relevant video evidence through a unified semantic interface, including interactive shot charts, filters, SPARQL queries, and natural-language questions through LLM-to-SPARQL. The underlying KG contains 9.5 M play-by-play-related triples covering 1063 games, while the interactive video catalogue currently provides synchronized access to 28 games from 3 EuroLeague seasons. Concerning evaluation, a manually annotated benchmark of 1833 actions from three EuroLeague games yields an overall median absolute temporal error of 4.0 s, with 57.72% and 68.46% of all actions localized within 5 s and 10 s, respectively. Notably, running-clock events (missed/made field goals, assists, rebounds, blocks, steals and turnovers) achieve higher accuracy with 81.04% localized within 5 s and 90.47% within 10 s, demonstrating the system’s effectiveness in temporally grounding actions during active gameplay. Finally, the offline grounding pipeline processes video at 22.74× real time, whereas the interactive CourtLens web application offers real-time interaction for video analysis, e.g., less than 1 s for filter-based search.

Longitudinal computational psychiatry aims to build computer models that track how a person's hidden mental health state changes over time using incomplete real-world clues like daily symptoms, behavior, physical data, and environment. While standard time-series models are great for tracking changing systems, they often break down when the number of hidden variables is large, measurements are missing, and different types of uncertainty overlap. This paper introduces a new method to estimate these hidden states cleanly and efficiently by breaking down complex updates into a sequence of simple, structured approximations.What Problem This SolvesTracking hidden mental states: In psychiatry, clinicians cannot directly measure a patient's underlying neurobiological or psychological state. Instead, models must infer these hidden states from indirect signals like smartphone usage, heart rate, sleep patterns, and self-reported mood.Handling messy, high-dimensional data: Real-world patient data is often incomplete, noisy, and spans many interacting variables. Updating a model's estimate of a patient's state when new data arrives requires complex calculations that become slow and unreliable as the number of variables grows.Borrowing from data compression: The authors adapt a technique originally designed for compressing images in generative AI. Instead of compressing pixels, they use the same logic to compress and simplify the adjustments a model makes when updating its belief about a patient's mental state.How the Sequential Codebook Method WorksDefining the update target: Whenever new patient data arrives, the model needs to adjust its previous estimate of the patient's hidden state. This adjustment is called the posterior state correction, and the goal is to approximate it using a limited, efficient amount of information.Building a menu of candidate updates: Rather than searching through infinite possibilities to fix its estimate, the model generates several independent "sections," or groups, of random candidate adjustments. Each candidate is shaped to respect the natural correlations and uncertainty patterns among the patient's hidden variables.Picking the best match step by step: In the first section, the model compares all available candidates against the current estimation error (the residual) and picks the single candidate that aligns best with what needs to be fixed. It then subtracts that adjustment and moves to the next section to fix whatever error remains.Predictable error reduction: Under ideal conditions, the authors prove that each sequential step reduces the remaining estimation error by a reliable, predictable fraction. Because each section works independently on the leftover error, adding more sections steadily shrinks the overall mistake at a guaranteed rate.Accounting for real-world digital limits: In theory, the weight given to each chosen candidate could be any continuous number. In practice, computers must round these weights to finite digital values (quantization), so the authors explicitly calculate how this rounding affects accuracy.Real-World Extensions and SafeguardsHandling missing data and shifting conditions: Longitudinal studies frequently suffer from missed check-ins or dead wearable batteries. The framework is expanded to handle missing data types and to remain accurate even when a patient's data patterns shift away from what the model originally expected.Clear rules and failure modes: The authors lay out the exact conditions required for their error-reduction guarantees to hold. They also examine when the model might fail or struggle to tell two different hidden causes apart (identifiability).A roadmap for testing: The authors emphasize that this framework is a proposed research method, not a ready-to-use clinical tool. To prove its worth, it must be tested on unseen patient data, checked for reliable uncertainty estimates, stripped down to test which parts actually matter, and compared directly against traditional tracking models.Core TakeawayBridging statistics and state estimation: The paper's main theoretical breakthrough is linking the statistics of extreme values in random bell-curve samples (Gaussian order statistics) to step-by-step error reduction. This provides a mathematically grounded way to update complex, uncertainty-weighted models of human mental health.
topics: Target Tracking and Data Fusion in Sensor Networks

documents.abstract: Authority Files in the Age of AI: Building Trustworthy Information Through Collaboration As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes how we conduct research and retrieve information, the need for trustworthy and reliable information has never been greater. Authority files have long played a vital role in improving precision and recall in information retrieval, traditionally in bibliographic catalogues and increasingly in research data as well. But what potential do they hold for AI applications, and how can they help ensure that AI systems provide reliable information? This presentation explores the role of authority files as a foundation for trustworthy AI applications. It highlights the importance of bringing together the knowledge and expertise of diverse communities to create a broader and more inclusive network of reference entities – without compromising the reliability and quality of the data. Using the cooperative framework of the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND) as an example, the presentation introduces an integrative infrastructure that enables communities to contribute their expertise to the collaborative creation and maintenance of authority data. Discover how collaboration, shared expertise and reliable authority data can help shape a more trustworthy information landscape in the age of AI. Please note: The PDF includes the complete speaker notes, providing additional explanations and context for a more comprehensive understanding of the presentation.

Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, complex spreadsheet tasks require both task reasoning and workbook understanding, while predefined operation interfaces impose additional tool-selection and invocation demands. We introduce SheetAlign, a spreadsheet manipulation framework with stage-isolated policy learning, organized around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations. Task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in workbook observations and available operations, while stage-isolated learning optimizes program generation and review using edit-progress rewards. At inference, execution consistency selects programs through agreement among workbook states. On SpreadsheetBench, our grounded task interface improves Qwen3-4B's accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without training. With learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign achieves 32.8% accuracy on average on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

Reinforcement learning (RL) with electronic design automation (EDA) feedback is advancing large language models for hardware design and verification. Extending these gains to hardware-engineering agents requires environments that span tasks, preserve state across tool calls, and support large hierarchies alongside parallel rollouts. We present SiliconGym, the first versatile, cross-task and cross-toolchain RL environment for hardware design and verification. By decoupling versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, SiliconGym scales from module-level RTL, testbench, and PPA tasks to multi-round repository repair and full-hierarchy SoC flows. Streaming dispatch overlaps tool checks with generation, finishing a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek. Using interchangeable open-source and commercial backends, we show that open-source-trained functional correctness transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, while paired netlist evaluation reveals when open-source PPA gains survive commercial synthesis.

documents.abstract: A one-pass decision encoder reads a text, a question and several named options, and returns a probability for each option in a single forward pass. We ask how far Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder of this kind, can be compressed before its decisions change. We count decisions that differ from Laya's own full-precision (fp32) answer, and track calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy, measured by expected calibration error, ECE), on 1,221 synthetic items with the training schemas, 273 with an unseen schema, and 800 out-of-family questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag. Layer pruning of a related model family is known; we add flips, calibration, held-out data and retraining. bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family decisions but 2.2% out of family; 6-bit grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%; deleting 6 layers 0.9% and 9.1%, while ECE rises from 5.9% to 39.2%. One fitted temperature, needing no labels, restores it to 3.6%. One scale per tensor fails below six bits, and CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, nearly all through one layer. Total variation tracks flips for rounding but not for deletion, and an early exit saves layers over a static cut only if its confidence gate is first recalibrated. Distilling a 16-layer student cuts its in-family flips from 44% to 9% (45% out of family). At equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than deletion. Data are synthetic and LLM-labelled, for one architecture.

Modern artificial intelligence paradigm designs overwhelmingly prioritize performance metrics, optimization velocity, and computational efficiency, reducing human oversight to post-hoc compliance mechanisms. This paper presents Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework), a governance standard engineered to re-establish human sovereignty as the primary, non-negotiable axiom of artificial intelligence architecture. Sittisart posits that human autonomy over personal data, context interpretation, and final decision-making must structurally precede algorithmic performance. We articulate a Four-Layer Rights Architecture (R1–R4)—comprising Data Sovereignty, Consent Integrity, Interpretation Rights, and the Right to Cut—complemented by Three System Integrity Laws. Together, these frameworks define verifiable operational boundaries that prevent opaque inference, silent profiling, and semantic collapse in intelligent systems, establishing a standardized blueprint for privacy-preserving, human-aligned AI deployment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png

Background/Objectives: Video-assisted CPR (V-CPR) improves the quality of CPR. Nevertheless, the available evidence has focused primarily on adult cardiac arrest scenarios and on compression-dominated resuscitation manoeuvres. In the paediatric setting, where ventilation is critical, the usefulness of V-CPR has scarcely been explored. We aimed to compare V-CPR using smartglasses and/or smartphones with each other and with voice-only assistance via smartphone in a simulated paediatric cardiac arrest. Methods: In this experimental pilot simulation study, thirty-four undergraduate sports science students without BLS training in the previous two years participated in a simulated cardiac arrest of an 8-year-old child, under dispatcher guidance. Participants received video-assistance using smartglasses (VA-SG), video-assistance using a smartphone (VA-Ph), or voice-only assistance (C). They performed 5 min of CPR (30:2 ratio). Assessments included CPR quality, response times, and CPR skills. Results: We showed that VA-Ph and VA-SG outperformed C in most outcomes. Significant differences were observed in the number of effective ventilations (p = 0.010) and chest compressions (CC) at correct depth (p = 0.006). Ventilation quality was 37.1 ± 32.9% in C, 70.1 ± 30.7% in VA-Ph, and 66.3 ± 28.9% in VA-SG (p = 0.038). CC quality reached 55.6 ± 28.0% in C, 74.0 ± 22.9% in VA-Ph, and 77.9 ± 16.6% in VA-SG (p = 0.150). Overall CPR quality was numerically higher in both video-assisted groups, although the difference was not statistically significant. V-CPR also improved correct CC hand placement (p = 0.001) and airway opening (p = 0.036). Response times did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions: Video-assistance via smartglasses or smartphones improves key components of the quality of dispatcher-guided CPR during simulated paediatric cardiac arrest, doubling effective ventilations and improving the proportion of compressions at correct depth, with no significant differences in time to CPR initiation. Direct scene visualisation gives dispatchers better situational awareness, enabling more accurate, real-time guidance that could translate into higher-quality resuscitation and improved outcomes.

documents.abstract: Socioeconomic differences in adolescents’ school belonging and school loneliness are important concerns for psychological adjustment. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into schoolwork, its associations with students’ school experiences and the moderating roles of relational resources warrant examination. This study used cross-sectional PISA data from adolescents in four Chinese regions. Unweighted multiple linear regression analyses examined economic, social and cultural status (ESCS) and AI use for schoolwork in relation to school loneliness and school belonging. Family support and peer academic help-seeking were examined separately as moderators of the associations between ESCS and each outcome. All models included sex, age, and school fixed effects. Multiple testing was addressed using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Higher ESCS and more frequent AI use for schoolwork were associated with lower school loneliness and greater school belonging. Peer academic help-seeking moderated the association between ESCS and school loneliness after FDR correction. The negative association weakened as peer academic help-seeking increased. Family support did not significantly moderate either association, and peer academic help-seeking did not significantly moderate the association between ESCS and school belonging. These findings suggest a limited compensatory role for peer academic help-seeking in socioeconomic differences in school loneliness, providing partial support for the resource compensation perspective.

Soil salinity is one of the major environmental constraints limiting agricultural productivity and global food security, affecting approximately 833 M ha of land worldwide. Its extent is increasing due to climate change, seawater intrusion, rock weathering, poor irrigation practices, inadequate drainage, groundwater over-extraction, excessive fertiliser use, irrigation with saline water and industrial effluent discharge. Salinity degrades soil structure, reduces nutrient availability, impairs photosynthesis, restricts plant growth and ultimately decreases crop productivity. This review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis of the causes, impacts, assessment methods and management strategies for soil salinity while highlighting recent advances in biotechnology and precision agriculture. Unlike previous reviews that focus on individual aspects of salinity, this review integrates conventional and emerging approaches within a single framework. Relevant literature was systematically identified and screened using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology to ensure transparent and comprehensive coverage. Recent advances in salinity assessment include remote sensing, electromagnetic induction (EMI), machine learning and geospatial techniques, enabling accurate large-scale monitoring and management of salt-affected soils. Effective mitigation strategies include improved irrigation and drainage, mulching, chemical amendments, silicon (Si) application, beneficial microorganisms, phytoremediation, nanotechnology and integrated soil management. Biotechnological approaches such as marker-assisted breeding, molecular breeding and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing have accelerated the development of salt-tolerant crop varieties, including BRRI dhan73, BRRI dhan99, CSR 101 and CSR 104. Future research should prioritise climate-resilient agriculture, sustainable land reclamation, precision farming and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technologies to enhance long-term salinity management and food security.

LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

Shoreline management in the Western Indian Ocean (WIO) is largely informed by small-scale studies with coarse temporal resolution, potentially obscuring fine spatial patterns and interannual dynamics. This study examines spatiotemporal shoreline change along 400 km of the Kenyan coastline from 2000 to 2024 and tests its association with regional sea-level trend and variability, accounting for spatial dependence. Twenty-five annual Landsat-derived shoreline positions were analyzed using the Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS) along 12,455 transects using Weighted Linear Regression (WLR) weighted by a tide- and registration-based positional uncertainty of approximately 40 to 68 m per epoch. Sea-level predictors were derived from GLORYS12V1 reanalysis at its native grid (47 coastal cells) and tested with Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), a Spatial Lag Model (SLM), and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR). Results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity. The Kilifi and Kwale–Mombasa zones show net accretion (mean WLR 0.57 and 0.51 m yr -1 , respectively), whereas the Tana–Manda zone shows net erosion (mean WLR = −0.92 m yr −1 ), with 36.23% of its transects significantly eroding. The national mean Net Shoreline Movement of +9.45 m obscures this variability. Shoreline change is strongly spatially autocorrelated (Moran’s I = 0.866, p = 0.001) and 12.01% of transects form statistically significant local clusters (6.23% as High–High accretion and 5.57% Low–Low erosion clusters). Neither sea-level trend nor sea-level variability showed a detectable association with shoreline change at the native support of the predictors (OLS R 2 ≤ 0.028, p ≥ 0.26; SLM not significant; GWR adjusted R 2 < 0). At the scales resolved here, shoreline change along the Kenyan coast is therefore not explained by regional sea-level variation and is more plausibly linked to local geomorphic and human factors. National averages must be complemented by spatially explicit, uncertainty-weighted assessments to inform shoreline management policy.

Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.

Autonomous AI agents increasingly decompose user instructions into task lists, but widely used approaches (AutoGPT, BabyAGI, MetaGPT) generate simple linear, ID-ordered sequences that cannot express conditional branching or parallel execution. Newer orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, the LLM Compiler, and the Claude Agent SDK add DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) or state-machine execution control for non-linear workflows, yet none provides a quantitative, probabilistic estimate of how likely a plan is to succeed, or how much a redundant (alternative) path improves that likelihood. This study integrates DAG-based dependency modeling, prompt engineering for conditional branching, and a state-machine execution engine, and formulates the resulting task-completion probability P(Goal) with reliability engineering. The model is generalized to 1-out-of-n (parallel) path redundancy and to general DAG topologies with parallel branching and AND-joins, and a cost-constrained redundancy-allocation problem and a Beta-prior estimator of path success probabilities from execution logs are given. Assuming independent task outcomes, Monte Carlo simulations (10,000–100,000 trials) of a retrieval-and-summarization task (72.7% completion for the linear model, 84.4% with redundancy) agree with the closed-form predictions to within 0.18 percentage points across 24 parameter combinations and within 1 point under all conditions. Redundancy at the bottleneck stage yields about 3.9 times the gain at the most reliable stage, as the marginal-utility formula predicts. Alternative paths help most when failures are persistent; correlated failures reduce the gain. With a real LLM agent (100 runs), completion rates predicted from probabilities estimated on half the runs fell within the 95% intervals observed on the other half.

The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.

documents.abstract: Teachers increasingly use generative artificial intelligence to prepare lessons, yet few accounts describe how teachers who are comfortable with digital tools do this successfully, what they still need, and how this looks in Philippine schools. This study documented the experiences of tech-savvy teachers in crafting lesson plans with artificial intelligence, the digital competencies they credited for their success, the challenges and strategies they reported, and the institutional support they recommended. A qualitative exploratory-descriptive design was used. Fifteen teachers of languages, mathematics, social science and social studies, organization and management, and agriculture, with 1 year 8 months to 16 years of teaching experience, were recruited through convenience and referral sampling and answered an online open-ended questionnaire. Tool use was summarized with frequencies and percentages, and the 58 written responses were analyzed through thematic analysis. ChatGPT (80%) and Google Gemini (66.7%) were the most used tools. Four themes emerged. First, fourteen teachers described planning with artificial intelligence as faster, easier, and more productive, and two noted effort at the outset, mainly in writing prompts. Second, success was linked to foundational digital literacy, prompt writing, and the ability to evaluate output, used together with teaching judgment. Third, the main challenges were output that did not fit learners, inaccurate information, and over-reliance, which teachers managed by reviewing, verifying, and localizing output. Fourth, teachers asked for continuous training, peer collaboration, and clear guidelines on appropriate use and its declaration. Interpreted through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework and technology acceptance theory, the findings suggest that these teachers’ success rested on their own judgment, prompting skill, and the support available to them. Because of the small sample, the brevity of many responses, and signs that some responses were machine-assisted, the findings are exploratory and not generalizable.

Sustainability-oriented entrepreneurship education is gaining traction, but few studies examine the mechanisms by which learning experiences translate into intentions to create socially and environmentally responsible businesses. Based on Human Capital Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour, this research investigates the mediating effect of sustainable opportunity recognition and green creativity sequentially and the moderating effect of Generative AI Literacy for Learning. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyse the survey responses of 407 students from public and private universities in Punjab, Pakistan. The findings showed a positive correlation between educational exposure and opportunity identification, which is linked to creative idea generation and, in turn, higher entrepreneurial intentions. The indirect (sequential) relationship is significant. Moreover, GenAI literacy strengthens both the education–intention and creativity–intention relationships, suggesting that technological competence complements sustainability-focused learning. These findings complement the existing explanations of entrepreneurial intention by adding an extension of the cognitive and creative process to a technology-related boundary condition. The study also underscores the importance of integrating sustainability problems, opportunities, innovative problem-solving, and responsible leveraging of generative AI into the curriculum, especially for higher education institutions, which are crucial for nurturing entrepreneurial aspirations in today's learning landscape.

This study aims to examine the challenges, implementation strategies, and benefits of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education and practice from 2021 to 2025. A systematic literature review was conducted using the PRISMA approach. Data were collected from the Scopus database. A Total of 17 articles met the inclusion criteria and then were analyzed using the PICOC framework. Findings indicate that the adoption of AI in vocational education and training not only faces technical issues but also challenges related to human readiness, institutional capacity, digital literacy, infrastructure gaps, and unequal access between developed and developing countries. Effective AI implementation requires an integrated strategy involving adaptive curriculum design, continuous training for educators, institutional leadership, industry collaboration, and the development of a supportive digital ecosystem. The integration of AI offers significant benefits in enhancing the quality of learning, the effectiveness of training, competency alignment, and workplace readiness, but its impact depends on how well the technology aligns with pedagogy, institutional readiness, and industry needs. Overall, the success of AI integration cannot be measured only by the technology used, but also by the capabilities of educational institutions and the creation of a collaborative ecosystem that is valuable to industry.

documents.abstract: With the large-scale implementation of generative artificial intelligence, digital twin, BIM and other technologies in the construction industry, the construction industry is transforming from the traditional manual construction mode to the intelligent construction mode, and the demand for industry post ability has changed significantly. As a core compulsory course of civil engineering undergraduate major, civil engineering construction undertakes the task of imparting professional knowledge such as construction technology, construction organization and site management. The traditional classroom teaching mode has practical contradictions such as lack of practical scenes, lagging update of teaching content, insufficient individualized training of students, and single assessment method. The teaching practice shows that the reasonable introduction of AI auxiliary tools can make up for the shortcomings of traditional teaching field conditions, enrich classroom case resources, and strengthen students’ engineering practice thinking. However, it also faces practical challenges such as students’ excessive dependence on AI output content, professional information distortion, and teachers’ teaching ability can not keep up with technical iteration. This study can provide reference for the digital teaching reform of construction courses in similar engineering majors, and help to cultivate compound civil engineering talents with both traditional construction skills and intelligent construction literacy.

Banks in emerging economies are under pressure to deliver faster, more personalised and more efficient digital financial services, yet many struggle to convert investments in artificial intelligence (AI) into innovation. This study examined how two dimensions of AI adoption readiness, technological readiness and organisational readiness, relate to product innovation and process innovation in deposit money banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and the Resource-Based View, the study adopted a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational survey of 400 employees and managers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Respondents rated organisational readiness (M = 3.62), process innovation (M = 3.59), product innovation (M = 3.54) and technological readiness (M = 3.45) above the scale midpoint. Both readiness dimensions correlated strongly and positively with both innovation outcomes (r = .68 to .74, p < .001). In multiple regression, the two predictors jointly explained 57.5% of the variance in product innovation and 56.7% in process innovation, and organisational readiness had the larger standardised coefficient in both models (β = .535 and .444) compared with technological readiness (β = .263 and .353). The findings indicate that technology is necessary but not sufficient for AI-enabled innovation. Banks should pair investment in infrastructure and skills with leadership sponsorship, employee training, a supportive culture and strategic alignment.

Context: The acceleration of digital transformation has reshaped learning environments in higher education and the conditions under which teachers and students engage in the learning process. This transformation creates opportunities while also posing challenges related to digital competencies, equity, and technological governance. Objective: To analyze the opportunities, challenges, and educational trends associated with the use of digital technologies in higher education. Method: A systematic literature review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and the Population, Interest, and Context (PICo) framework. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, SciELO, ERIC, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 25 empirical studies published between 2022 and September 2026. Results: The findings identified learning flexibility and personalization, the early adoption of generative artificial intelligence, and the growing importance of teachers' digital competence as major educational trends. Disparities in access were also observed, influenced by technological infrastructure and training opportunities. Blended learning and ethical technology governance emerged as key elements in guiding institutional transformation. Conclusions: The effective pedagogical integration of digital technologies in higher education requires coherent institutional policies, continuous professional development for faculty members, and critical digital literacy across the university community. Technological transformation must be accompanied by strategies aimed at narrowing digital access gaps and ensuring educational integration that is contextually relevant, equitable, and responsible.

As transformações tecnológicas associadas à Indústria 4.0, à saúde digital e à inteligência artificial ampliaram o repertório da Fisioterapia do Trabalho e da Ergonomia, permitindo que avaliações antes pontuais sejam complementadas por monitoramento contínuo, análise automatizada de posturas e intervenções remotas. Este trabalho discute, sob a perspectiva da prática baseada em evidências, o papel de sensores vestíveis, unidades de medição inercial, inteligência artificial, visão computacional, exoesqueletos ocupacionais, telereabilitação, estações de trabalho ativas e programas de exercício no enfrentamento dos distúrbios osteomusculares relacionados ao trabalho. A revisão priorizou estudos indexados publicados entre 2020 e 2026, com ênfase em revisões sistemáticas, meta-análises, ensaios clínicos e revisões de escopo, além da Norma Regulamentadora nº 17 como referência normativa brasileira. Os achados mostram que intervenções ergonômicas e exercício no local de trabalho possuem evidência mais consolidada para redução de dor e melhora funcional; tecnologias vestíveis e sistemas automatizados ampliam a capacidade de mensurar exposição biomecânica em tempo real, mas ainda apresentam heterogeneidade de validação; exoesqueletos reduzem carga muscular em tarefas específicas, embora conforto, adaptação e transferência dos resultados de laboratório para o campo permaneçam limitadas; e a telereabilitação apresenta resultados clínicos comparáveis ou favoráveis em diferentes condições musculoesqueléticas. Conclui-se que a alta performance ocupacional deve ser entendida como desempenho sustentável, com preservação da saúde, redução de fadiga, retorno seguro ao trabalho e melhor capacidade funcional, e não como intensificação indiscriminada da produção. A integração tecnológica é mais efetiva quando subordinada à análise ergonômica, à participação do trabalhador e à tomada de decisão clínica baseada na melhor evidência disponível.

documents.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important area of research as AI systems are increasingly used to support cybersecurity decisions. Providing explanations for AI-generated recommendations can improve transparency, help users understand system outputs, and support greater confidence in automated decisions. However, increasing the amount of information provided by an AI system may also create additional cognitive demands for users, particularly when explanations contain complex technical information. This paper examines the AI explainability paradox in cybersecurity, focusing on the relationship between explanation complexity, cognitive load, human understanding, and security decision-making. Drawing on existing literature related to explainable AI, cognitive load, human-AI interaction, cybersecurity decision-making, and technology trust, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI explanation, information complexity, cognitive load, user understanding, verification behaviour, and decision quality. The paper proposes that effective explainability should not be determined only by the amount of information provided, but also by the ability of users to understand and effectively use that information during security-related decisions. While appropriate explanations may improve transparency and support informed judgement, excessive or technically complex explanations may increase cognitive load and reduce decision effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI explanation influence human cybersecurity decisions and contributes to the development of human-centred explainable AI systems.

Today, businesses are making more and more use of Artificial Intelligent (AI) technologies in their operations. This widespread use of AI technologies is changing how a consumer searches, evaluates and purchases products in the online intelligent markets. Consumer behavior is shaped by consumer’s own cognition as well as influence by machine learning systems (AI technologies). These advanced systems use algorithmic personalization, predictive analysis, ranking systems and automated decision support to guide the consumers. To understand the consumer buying behavior in these intelligent markets, this paper, titled “The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets,” proposes an integrated conceptual framework. “Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al. 2003)”, “Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers, 2003)” and “Disruptive Innovation Perspectives (Christensen, 1997)” are the foundations of this research. This paper argues that the algorithmic influence works through three interconnected mechanisms namely, behavioral reinforcement through personalization, cognitive effort reduction and perceived performance enhancement. Here, conventional consumer behavior models are extended by adding new constructs such as algorithmic trust, perceived AI transparency, adaptive habit formation and data-driven social influence. This paper proposes that AI tools and systems do not simply play the role of marketing tools but also actively influence consumer preferences, attention, post-purchase learning and habits. In this work, theory is being built methodologically and conceptual synthesis technique is used. Model abstraction (simplification) and comparison analysis is used to achieve proposed conceptual integration. A through multidisciplinary analysis which included literature from marketing, information systems and innovation studies, was carried out. The aim of this exercise was to identify overlapping theoretical frameworks. With this exercise a nested framework is created that connect behavioral results, psychological mediators and technology affordances. Traditional consumer theories have been used, which focus on the human-centric framework as a base for this exercise. This base was further expanded to understand AI-augmented viewpoint. This study strongly proposes that AI tools & systems are actively involved in the consumer’s decisions-making journey as opposed to the previous conception of them being simply passive actors, guiding consumers. The implications of this study highlight that organizations must manage system transparency, trust alignment and personalization to maximize consumer engagement. This study describes “algorithmic consumer” and its inception. Going further, this study also lays foundation for future empirical studies as well as policy discussions of autonomy, ethics, and control over pricing in the AI-powered digital ecosystems.

Objective: This study aims to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) system based on the U-Net deep learning architecture to automatically identify and stage lymphatic vessels in indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography images, thereby enhancing recognition efficiency and objectivity and assisting in the planning of lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) surgery. Methods: A total of 560 ICG lymphography images from 140 patients with lower-limb lymphedema were collected. After standard preprocessing, the images were randomly split into a training set and a test set in a 7:3 ratio. The U-Net model was used for training, with hyperparameters optimized using a five-fold cross-validation approach. The Adam optimizer was employed for model training. Evaluation metrics included precision, recall, F1 score, and inference time. Results: The model demonstrated excellent performance in identifying lymphatic vessels across lymphedema stages I–IV. The precision scores for each stage were as follows: stage I: 95.29%, stage II: 92.58%, stage III: 93.17%, and stage IV: 90.08%. Recall rates for all stages were above 89%, and all F1 scores exceeded 90%, indicating strong overall accuracy and balance between precision and recall. The average inference time per image was just 56 milliseconds, highlighting the model’s suitability for near-real-time applications. Additionally, the confusion matrix revealed a high discriminative capability across the different lymphedema stages. Conclusion: The U-Net-based AI model demonstrated high accuracy and efficiency in the automatic identification of lymphatic vessels in ICG images, highlighting its strong potential for clinical applications. This system may significantly support LVA surgical planning, enable real-time intraoperative navigation, and serve as a valuable tool for physician training.
